readerTitle: Why a 15% price cut shrank a box maker's revenue
caseNote: 가상 사례 (골판지 상자 제조사, 팀 일정관리 앱) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가격을 바꾸기 전에 '얼마나 싸게/비싸게'보다 '고객이 얼마나 반응할까'를 먼저 묻는다. 같은 제품도 고객이 다르면 반응이 다르다.
misconception: 가격을 내리면 판매량이 늘어 매출이 오른다. 가격을 올리면 고객이 떠나 매출이 준다.

sources.text: 미시경제학의 표준 개념 (수요의 가격탄력성 = 수요량 변화율 ÷ 가격 변화율)

factChecks.note: 수요를 움직이는 요인 목록(대체재, 예산 비중, 전환 비용, 시간)은 교과서 표준 설명입니다. 필수재·사치재 구분은 형제 레슨 ECO-04-02에서 다루므로 여기서는 제외했습니다.

cards.title: Why a 15% price cut shrank a box maker's revenue
body: A maker of plain shipping boxes cut its price by 15% to win more orders. Orders rose by 3%.
Revenue fell. Profit fell by more than a third. The plan was logical. The customers just didn't behave the way it assumed.

image.label: Stacks of cardboard boxes beside a falling revenue arrow
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 공장 바닥에 평범한 골판지 상자가 쌓여 있고, 상자 더미 위에 "−15%" 가격표. 옆에는 아래로 꺾이는 매출 화살표. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Will a cheaper box sell more boxes?
body: You sell plain shipping boxes at $1.00 each, about 100,000 a month. Your customers are food and electronics makers. A box is about 1% of what their products cost, and switching suppliers means re-testing boxes on their packing lines.
You're thinking of cutting the price to $0.85. What happens?

options.text: Orders jump by 20% or more, and revenue rises
options.feedback: That's the hopeful version. It assumes customers want more boxes, but they only need as many as they have products to ship.

options.text: Orders barely move, and revenue falls
options.feedback: Right. A cheaper box doesn't make customers ship more goods, and switching is a hassle. You give up 15c on every box and gain few new ones.

options.text: Orders rise just enough to keep revenue about flat
options.feedback: You'd need about 18% more boxes just to break even on revenue. With these customers, nothing points to that kind of jump.

cards.title: The month after the cut.
body: Customers ship as many boxes as they have products to ship. A cheaper box doesn't create more products.

cards.title: Price elasticity
body: **Price elasticity** measures how strongly the amount people buy reacts to a change in price. Divide the % change in quantity by the % change in price.
Here: 3% ÷ 15% = 0.2. Below 1, demand is *inelastic*: price cuts lose revenue and price rises gain it. Above 1, demand is *elastic*, and the reverse is true.

image.label: A stiff spring and a stretchy spring under the same price push
image.brief: 두 개의 스프링 비교 인포그래픽. 같은 크기의 손이 "Price −15%"로 누르는데, 왼쪽 단단한 스프링은 거의 안 늘어남("Inelastic: 0.2"), 오른쪽 부드러운 스프링은 크게 늘어남("Elastic: 2.5"). 단순한 색 블록 스타일.

cards.title: What makes demand stretch or stiffen.
body: A few things decide how much buyers react to a price change:
list: **Substitutes:** can buyers easily get something similar elsewhere?
**Share of budget:** is your price a big or tiny part of what they spend?
**Switching effort:** does changing supplier take testing, contracts or retraining?
**Time:** buyers often react more over months than over days
cards.callout: The box maker's customers had little reason to react, so the cut bought almost nothing.

cards.title: Same factory, different customers.
body: The company also sells printed boxes to small online shops at $2.00. These buyers compare quotes online and can switch with a few clicks.
A 10% cut there brought 25% more orders. Elasticity: 25% ÷ 10% = **2.5**. Revenue rose 12.5%.
Same boxes, same factory. The cut failed in one market and worked in the other, because the buyers were different.

image.label: Two customer groups reacting differently to the same price tag
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눔. 왼쪽은 대형 공장 구매 담당자 한 명이 가격표를 보고도 무덤덤함("+3%"). 오른쪽은 노트북 앞 소규모 온라인 판매자 여러 명이 몰려옴("+25%"). 실제 로고·상표 없음.

cards.title: Elastic doesn't mean profitable.
body: Say each printed box costs $1.40 to make. Before the cut, each left $0.60. After, $0.40. Even with 25% more orders, that's $0.50 per original order instead of $0.60. Revenue up, profit down about 17%.
Elasticity also moves. It changes at different price levels, over time, and when rivals match you. Test on a small group before changing prices for everyone.

cards.title: Now it's a software subscription.
body: Your team-planning app costs $20 per user a month. For one month, you show $24 to half of new sign-ups. That group signs up 5% less often than the $20 group.

options.text: Keep $20. Losing 5% of sign-ups is too costly
options.feedback: That protects sign-up numbers but leaves money on the table: 95 users at $24 bring $2,280, versus $2,000 from 100 users at $20.

options.text: Move new customers to $24 and track cancellations for a few months
options.feedback: An elasticity of about 0.25 says demand is inelastic near this price. Tracking cancellations checks whether paying users react more slowly than new sign-ups.

options.text: Jump straight to $30, since users barely react
options.feedback: The direction is right, but a test between $20 and $24 says little about $30. Buyers often get more sensitive as the price climbs.

cards.title: Before you change a price, ask how much buyers will react.
body: Price elasticity tells you whether a cut buys real volume or just gives money away, and whether a rise drives customers off or simply earns more.
**Try it today:** pick one product. Write down how easily your customers could switch, how big your price is in their budget, and how you think they'd react to a 10% change.
